newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown loses some of its lustre-Goldman Sachs.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown loses some of its lustre-Goldman Sachs.

text.p: The Czech crown has lost some of the lustre that has made it one of Europe's most attractive currency trades over the last 18 months, an investor report from Goldman Sachs said.
The report, issued on September 24, said that several developments in the external, fiscal, and financial sectors warrant "a more conservative view toward the market".

"We note in particular a deterioration in trade performance and composition of capital flows; an easing of monetary policy; a weakening of the banking system; and an increase in political risk," the report said.
It said that trade and current account deficits have widened "considerably" while net capital inflows, particularly foreign direct investment, have slowed.
The foreign trade deficit hit a record 100.9 billion crowns for the January-August period, compared to 59.5 billion over the same period last year.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) recently revised its 1996 full year forecast for the trade deficit to reach around 143 billion and for the current account deficit to be 5.7 percent of GDP.
The current account deficit in the first half was $1.7 billion compared to a $723 million shortfall for the first six months of 1995.

The report added that while the Czech National Bank (CNB) remains committed to tackling inflation, "the ongoing weakness of the Czech banking sector is likely both to divert its attention from monetary policy and discourage any moves toward higher interest rates".
In August, the CNB rescinded the licence of the insolvent Kreditni Banka with losses estimated at nearly 12 billion crowns after a complicated series of non-performing loans and debt swaps.

It then followed in mid-September with the temporary forced administration of Agrobanka -- the 12th bank to come under CNB supervision -- saying it had become illiquid partly because of its ties to Kreditni and the secretive investment group Motoinvest.

The loss of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's parliamentary majority in general elections in the spring is also clouding the crown's outlook according to the report, and political uncertainty is bound to increase in the run-up to key Senate elections November 15-16.
"We believe the economic policies so far pursued by Mr. Klaus's government would largely be maintained regardless of the electoral outcome," the report said.
"Recalling the need for CNB intervention to support the crown in the run-up to the June elections, we recognise that the increased political uncertainty could marginally affect the exchange rate."
